title: Cleaning the corpus
objectives: Write exact and near-duplicate filters for a text corpus.

screens.title: Exact deduplication
screens.prose: **Exact deduplication** keeps a set of the lines (or their hashes) seen so far; a line already in the set is a repeat. Duplicates matter. A model memorises text it sees many times, and a test passage copied into training flatters the test score.
screens.question: How many non-empty lines are repeats of an earlier line?

hints.text: Each distinct line is kept once.
Every other non-empty line is a repeat.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Subtract the distinct lines from all the lines.

byKey.distinct: That is the number of lines kept. The repeats are the rest.

explain.text: Each of the 25,721 distinct lines is kept once, so $32777 - 25721 = 7056$ lines are repeats. A set makes each check fast, whatever the size of the text.

screens.title: What the repeats are
screens.prose: Call a line a speaker tag when it ends in a colon and follows a blank line. In the full text, 6,913 of the 7,056 repeated lines are speaker tags.
screens.question: What percentage of the repeated lines are speaker tags? Give one decimal place.

hints.text: Divide the tags by all the repeats.

feedback.correct: About 98.0%: nearly every repeated line is a speaker tag.

byKey.of-all: You divided by all 32,777 lines. The question asks about the repeated lines only.
byKey.others: That is the share of repeats that are not tags, 143 of 7,056.

explain.text: $6913 / 7056 \approx 0.980$, so 98.0% of the repeats are tags. Only 143 repeated lines are speech, such as `Farewell.` said twice.

screens.title: The wrong unit
screens.prose: Deleting the 7,056 repeated lines would strip almost every speaker tag after its first use. Most speeches would lose their speaker.
screens.question: At what unit should a cleaner look for duplicates in a corpus like this?

options.text: Whole documents, such as a play or a scene
Lines, because that removes the most repetition
options.why: You picked the unit that finds the most repeats. 98% of them are speaker tags, so this deletes structure, not repetition.

options.text: Words, keeping each word once
options.why: Every common word repeats. Keeping each word once would destroy the text.

options.text: Characters
options.why: Only 65 distinct characters appear; deduplicating them leaves 65 characters.

hints.text: A repeat is a problem when the same content appears twice.
Is a repeated speaker tag repeated content?
Look for whole documents that appear twice.

feedback.correct: Documents: a play copied twice is a duplicate; a speaker named twice is not.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Choose the unit at which a repeat means repeated content.

byKey.lines: Line-level cleaning would delete 6,913 speaker tags. Choose the unit at which a match means the same content was copied.

explain.text: Repetition that hurts is a whole document copied, such as a web page scraped twice. Check at the document level, so structure inside a document survives.

screens.title: Shingles
screens.prose:
A **shingle** is a run of $n$ characters. Two texts that share most shingles are nearly the same. Take this news story, 92 characters long.

`Shell shares rose 2% to £27.10 on Tuesday after the oil major raised its quarterly dividend.`

state.caption: The first 12 characters: each shingle starts one place after the last.

screens.question: How many 5-character shingles does the story have? Every one is different.

hints.text: A shingle can start at any position that leaves 5 characters.
The last shingle starts at position 87, counting from 0.
Positions 0 to 87: $92 - 5 + 1 = 88$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the starting positions that leave room for 5 characters.

byKey.chars: That is the number of characters. The last four cannot start a 5-character shingle.
byKey.off-by-one: Off by one: positions 0 to 87 make 88 starts.

explain.text: A text of 92 characters has $92 - 5 + 1 = 88$ starting positions for a 5-character shingle. When all are different, the set has 88 shingles.

screens.title: Jaccard similarity
screens.prose: A second story is the same except that the price reads £27.40. The **Jaccard similarity** of two shingle sets is the shared shingles over all the different shingles.
screens.question: What is the Jaccard similarity of the two stories? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: Shared over in either.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the shared shingles by the shingles in either set.

byKey.over-one: You divided by one story's 88 shingles. Jaccard divides by the union, 93.
byKey.sum: You divided by the sum of the sizes, which counts the shared shingles twice. Use the union.

explain.text: Changing one digit breaks the 5 shingles that cover it, in each story: 88 - 5 = 83 are shared and 83 + 5 + 5 = 93 are in either. So $J = 83 / 93 \approx 0.8925$.

screens.title: Near duplicates with different facts
screens.prose: A near-duplicate filter drops one of any two stories with Jaccard similarity above 0.8. The two Shell stories score 0.8925.
screens.question: What does the filter do to a training set for a model that should report prices?

options.text: It drops a story whose price differs: a real fact
Nothing harmful: the stories are near copies
options.why: They are near copies in wording, but they state different prices. One of the two facts is lost.

options.text: It keeps both, because they are not identical
options.why: The filter uses a threshold of 0.8, and 0.8925 is above it.

options.text: It merges the two stories into one
options.why: A filter keeps or drops; it never merges texts.

hints.text: Is the Jaccard value above the threshold?
What differs between the stories?
The filter drops one, and with it one of the two prices.

feedback.correct: The filter sees near copies and drops one, losing a real fact.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare the score with 0.8, then ask what the stories disagree on.

explain.text: Shingles measure wording, not meaning. Two reports that differ in one number look like duplicates; a filter for facts must check the numbers too.

screens.title: Measuring overlap
screens.prose:
For shingle sets $A$ and $B$:
$$J(A, B) = \frac{|A \cap B|}{|A \cup B|}$$
It is 1 for identical sets and 0 for disjoint ones. Comparing every pair of a billion documents is too slow. Real pipelines use **MinHash**, which estimates $J$ from short signatures; we name it and do not build it.
screens.question: Two documents share every shingle, but one also has 10 shingles of its own. What can you say about $J$?

options.text: It is below 1, because the union is larger than the shared part
It is 1, because every shingle of the smaller one is shared
options.why: Jaccard divides by the union. The 10 extra shingles make the union larger than the shared set.

options.text: It is 0, because the documents differ
options.why: Jaccard is 0 only when no shingle is shared.

options.text: It is 0.5 whatever the sizes
options.why: It depends on how many shingles are shared against how many there are in all.

hints.text: Write $|A \cap B|$ and $|A \cup B|$ for the two documents.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare the shared set with the union.

explain.text: The smaller set $A$ is inside the larger, so $J = |A| / (|A| + 10)$, below 1. Only identical sets reach 1.

screens.title: Write the exact filter
screens.prose: Write `dedup_lines(text)`. Split on `'\n'`, skip empty lines and keep each line the first time it appears. Return `(kept, removed)`: the kept lines in order, and the count of non-empty lines dropped.

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests: small texts with repeats, blank lines, and near misses that differ in case or a trailing space. The last reads the whole Shakespeare slice and checks the kept count, the removed count and the first four kept lines.

mutants.symptom: Treats blank lines as lines, so repeated blanks count as removed.
Ignores case, so lines that differ in case are merged.
Counts each repeated line once, not each repeat.

hints.text: Keep a set of lines already seen.
A line already in the set adds 1 to `removed`; a new line goes into the set and onto `kept`.
Loop over `text.split('\n')`, `continue` on `''`, then check membership in the set.

feedback.correct: On the slice you keep 5,920 lines and remove 1,686.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-4: Test 4 is only blank lines. Skip them; they are neither kept nor counted as removed.
byKey.test-6: Test 6 has lines that differ only in case or a trailing space. Exact deduplication treats them as different.

explain.text: A set makes each check cost about the same whatever the text's size. On the slice, 1,686 of 7,606 non-empty lines are repeats, and nearly all are speaker tags.

screens.title: Shingles and Jaccard in code
screens.prose: Write `shingles(text, n)`, the set of every run of `n` characters in `text`, and `jaccard(a, b)` for two sets, not both empty.
screens.question: Write `shingles` and `jaccard`.

tests.call: len(shingles('Shell shares rose 2% to £27.10 on Tuesday after the oil major raised its quarterly dividend.', 5))

jaccard(shingles('Shell shares rose 2% to £27.10 on Tuesday after the oil major raised its quarterly dividend.', 5), shingles('Shell shares rose 2% to £27.40 on Tuesday after the oil major raised its quarterly dividend.', 5))

widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests: shingles of short strings, a string shorter than `n`, a run of one letter and the price story. Jaccard values on small sets and on the two stories are accepted within a relative 1e-9. The sets in the tests are never both empty.

mutants.symptom: Divides by the sum of the sizes, counting shared shingles twice.
Returns a list, so repeated shingles are counted again.

hints.text: A set comprehension over the starting positions builds the shingles.
Start positions run from 0 to `len(text) - n`.
`{text[i:i + n] for i in range(len(text) - n + 1)}`, and `len(a & b) / len(a | b)`.

feedback.correct: Your sets and scores match: 0.8925 for the two stories.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-3: Test 3 has a text shorter than `n`, which has no shingles: return an empty set.
byKey.test-9: Test 9 is the two stories. Divide by the union `a | b`, not by one set's size.

explain.text: `range(len(text) - n + 1)` gives every start, and a set drops repeats. Jaccard is then two set operations and a division.

screens.title: One note, three distributors
screens.prose: A research team collects broker notes. One note arrives through three distributors, each adding a header or footer. The same broker also sends a second note. The table gives each pair's Jaccard similarity over 5-character shingles.

state.caption: A, B and C carry the same note; D is the broker's other note.

screens.question: With a threshold of 0.8, tap every pair the filter flags as near duplicates.

hints.text: Flag a pair when its Jaccard similarity is 0.8 or more.
The three copies of one note score far above the pairs with D.
Rows A and B, A and C, and B and C.

feedback.correct: The three copies of the note are flagged; the second note is kept.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Tap only the rows at 0.8 or above.

byKey.with-d: You flagged every pair. The pairs with D share only the broker's boilerplate and score well below 0.8.

explain.text: The copies differ only in headers and a footer, so they score high; two of the three are dropped. Note D shares the broker's phrasing but not its content, so it stays.

ideas: Exact deduplication keeps a set of what it has seen; duplicates make a model memorise and can leak a test set into training.
Choose the unit with care: 98% of Tiny Shakespeare's repeated lines are speaker tags, so deduplicate documents, not lines.
Near duplicates share most shingles: Jaccard similarity $|A \cap B| / |A \cup B|$, estimated at scale by MinHash; a near copy can still carry a different fact.

formula.name: Jaccard similarity
formula.note: $A$ and $B$ are shingle sets, not both empty.

summary.trap: Deduplicating at the wrong unit: line-level cleaning of a play deletes its speaker tags, which are structure, not repetition.

quiz.prose: The course's slice of Tiny Shakespeare has 7,606 non-empty lines, of which 5,920 are distinct.
quiz.question: How many lines does exact line deduplication remove?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Subtract the distinct lines from all the lines.

byKey.kept: That is the number kept. Removed is the rest.

explain.text: Each distinct line is kept once, so $7606 - 5920 = 1686$ are removed, nearly all speaker tags.

quiz.prose: A team scores its model on a test set of news paragraphs. Later it finds that 30% of the test paragraphs also appear, word for word, in the training data.
quiz.question: What does that do to the reported test score?

options.text: It makes the score look better than the model would do on new text
Nothing: a paragraph is scored the same wherever it appears
options.why: A model can memorise text it trained on. Its loss on those paragraphs is lower than on unseen ones.

options.text: It makes the score look worse
options.why: Seen text is easier for the model, not harder.

options.text: It changes only the 30% and averages out
options.why: The 30% pull the average down, so the whole test loss is too low.

feedback.correct: Leaked test text is partly memorised, so the test loss is too low.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What can a model do with text it trained on?

explain.text: A test set must be unseen. Paragraphs copied into training are partly memorised, so the test score overstates how the model does on new text.

quiz.question: How many distinct 3-character shingles does `aaaa` have?

feedback.generic: Not quite. List the shingles, then remove repeats.

byKey.positions: There are 2 starting positions, but both give `aaa`; a set keeps it once.

explain.text: Positions 0 and 1 both give `aaa`, so the set holds 1 shingle. Shingle sets count distinct runs, not positions.
